chunks: Components that need more PCB layers. The question: What components would require a higher layer count?
Some parts force a board to have more layers. A dense chip with hundreds of tiny solder balls underneath needs room to route every signal out.
Fast interfaces like DDR memory need a solid copper plane next to each routing layer. Chips with many supply voltages need extra power layers.
Simple parts like small microcontrollers do not, which is why a hobby board can have only two layers.
Imagine a packed stadium with narrow aisles. Each aisle holds only so many people side by side, so the crowd in the middle cannot all leave at once.
You would need several tiers of walkways to get everyone out.
A dense chip is the crowd, the gaps between its pads are the aisles, and each board layer is another tier of walkways.
The analogy is loose: a board also needs whole layers for planes that carry no signals at all.
With a 0. 8 mm pitch only one trace fits between the via pads, so each signal layer can free about two rows. Smaller features cost money; this is a fab-capability decision.
BGA (ball grid array): a chip package with a grid of solder balls underneath it. Pitch: the center-to-center distance between neighboring balls.
Via pad: the round copper landing of a plated hole that takes a signal to another layer.
Escape routing: getting each signal out from under the chip ("Choosing the PCB layer count").
Power domain: a separate supply voltage that needs its own distribution ("Which layers for power planes").
Take a 22 by 22 grid (484 balls) at 1. 0 mm pitch, with 0. 55 mm via pads. The gap between pads is 1. 0 - 0. 55 = 0. 45 mm. A 0. 1 mm trace with 0.
1 mm of space on each side needs 0. 30 mm, so one trace fits, but two (0. 50 mm) do not. With one trace per gap, each layer frees about 2 rows.
The middle 8 by 8 balls are power and ground, leaving (22 - 8)/2 = 7 signal rows from the edge in. That needs about 4 signal layers, with planes on top of that.
That is the whole idea.
"Dense, fast or power-hungry parts push the layer count up. Fine-pitch BGAs need extra layers to escape their signals, roughly two rows of balls per layer at 0. 8 mm pitch.
High-speed interfaces like DDR, PCIe and USB 3 need a reference plane next to each routing layer. Processors and FPGAs with many rails need power planes and decoupling space.
RF and mixed-signal sections need isolation, and big connectors need layers for sheer pin count. Simple QFP microcontrollers and regulators don't."
